title: Capstone Project: Build and Deploy an End-to-End AI System
summary: The capstone ties everything together into one portfolio-worthy project. You will choose a real problem, gather and prepare data, train and evaluate a model (classical ML or an LLM-powered feature), then serve it via a FastAPI API, containerize it wi
content:
# Capstone Project: Build and Deploy an End-to-End AI System ##### The 96% model that shipped nothing Two students finished the same course. Both built a churn predictor. The first spent six weeks on modelling. They tried nine algorithms, ran an extensive hyperparameter sweep, and reached 96% accuracy — genuinely impressive work, presented as a Jupyter notebook. The second reached 87% in four days with gradient boosting, then spent five weeks on everything else: a FastAPI service, a Docker image, deployment to Cloud Run with a public URL, prediction logging, a drift check, a CI pipeline, and a README with a before/after impact estimate. In interviews, the first candidate was asked "how would you deploy this?" and had no answer. The second sent a URL that the interviewer clicked. **The capstone is not a modelling exercise.** Nine percentage points of accuracy is worth less than a deployed, monitored, documented system, because the second demonstrates every skill this course covered and the first demonstrates one. ##### Choosing a problem Three criteria, and getting this right saves weeks. **Data must already exist and be accessible.** Do not plan a project that requires scraping a site you have not tested or an API you have not been granted. Verify you can load the data on day one. **The scope must fit the time.** One model, one clear prediction task, one deployment target. "A recommendation engine with real-time personalization and A/B testing" is three projects. **You should care about the outcome.** You will debug this at 11 p.m., and curiosity is what carries you through. Problem types that work well, with honest notes: | Project | Data source | Watch out for | |---|---|---| | Document Q&A assistant | Your own PDFs | Chunking quality determines everything | | Support ticket triage | Public datasets, or synthesize | Class imbalance | | Price/demand forecasting | Kaggle, government open data | Must split chronologically | | Image classifier | Domain photos, transfer learning | Class imbalance, augmentation | | Resume/job matcher | Synthetic or public | Bias audit is mandatory here | | Churn prediction | Telco/banking public datasets | Temporal leakage | Write a **one-paragraph problem statement** before any code, and make it specific about the decision the model improves: > *"Support agents spend roughly 3 minutes triaging each of ~400 daily tickets. A classifier that routes tickets by category and urgency, with low-confidence cases escalated to humans, should cut triage time to under 30 seconds per ticket while maintaining above 90% routing accuracy."* That paragraph gives you a metric, a baseline and a success criterion — three things that make the final write-up possible. ##### Phase 1: Data and baseline Do the unglamorous parts first, because they determine what is achievable. ```python # Day 1-2: establish that the problem is solvable at all df = load_data() print(df.shape, df.dtypes, df.isna().mean().round(3), sep="\n") print(df["target"].value_counts(normalize=True)) # class balance # CRITICAL: split before anything else if is_temporal: cutoff = df["date"].quantile(0.8) train, test = df[df.date <= cutoff], df[df.date > cutoff] else: train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, stratify=df.target, random_state=42) # Baseline FIRST — what does "no model" achieve? from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(X_train, y_train) print(f"Baseline: {f1_score(y_test, baseline.predict(X_test), average='macro'):.3f}") ``` The **baseline is not optional**. If your sophisticated model cannot beat majority-class prediction, something is wrong with the features, the labels or the framing — and you want to know that on day two, not week five. Establish your **metric** here too, chosen from the cost of errors rather than habit. For imbalanced triage, macro-F1 or per-class recall; for forecasting, MAE in the original units so stakeholders understand it. ##### Phase 2: Model Give this less time than instinct suggests. A well-tuned gradient boosting model on good features beats a poorly-featured neural network almost every time on tabular data. ```python from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer import joblib, json preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([ ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric_features), ("cat", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")), ("enc", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first"))]), categorical_features), ]) model = Pipeline([("prep", preprocessor), ("clf", XGBClassifier(n_estimators=1000, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=5, subsample=0.8, early_stopping_rounds=50, random_state=42))]) model.fit(X_train, y_train, clf__eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], clf__verbose=False) # Save the WHOLE pipeline plus metadata joblib.dump(model, "models/model_v1.joblib", compress=3) Path("models/model_v1.json").write_text(json.dumps({ "version": "1.0.0", "trained_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__, "metrics": {"test_f1_macro": test_f1, "baseline_f1": baseline_f1}, "feature_columns": list(X_train.columns), "n_training_samples": len(X_train), }, indent=2)) ``` Saving the **whole Pipeline** rather than just the estimator is what makes serving trivial — the API accepts raw feature values and preprocessing travels with the model. The metadata file is what lets you answer "which model is this and how good was it?" six months later. Stop when you hit diminishing returns. **Three days of tuning for two percentage points is three days not spent on deployment**, and deployment is what the capstone is actually assessing. ##### Phase 3: Serve ```python from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Depends, status from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ConfigDict from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from typing import Literal import time, uuid, joblib, json, logging log = logging.getLogger(__name__) artifacts: dict = {} @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app: FastAPI): artifacts["model"] = joblib.load("models/model_v1.joblib") artifacts["meta"] = json.loads(Path("models/model_v1.json").read_text()) artifacts["model"].predict_proba(SAMPLE_FRAME) # warm-up log.info("model loaded: %s", artifacts["meta"]["version"]) yield artifacts.clear() app = FastAPI(title="Ticket Triage API", version="1.0.0", lifespan=lifespan) class TicketRequest(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid") subject: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200) body: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=5000) customer_tier: Literal["free", "pro", "enterprise"] prior_tickets: int = Field(ge=0, le=1000) class TriageResponse(BaseModel): category: str confidence: float = Field(ge=0, le=1) needs_human: bool model_version: str prediction_id: str latency_ms: float @app.post("/v1/triage", response_model=TriageResponse) def triage(req: TicketRequest) -> TriageResponse: pid, start = str(uuid.uuid4()), time.perf_counter() try: frame = pd.DataFrame([req.model_dump()]) probs = artifacts["model"].predict_proba(frame)[0] idx = int(probs.argmax()) category = artifacts["model"].classes_[idx] confidence = float(probs[idx]) except Exception as exc: log.exception("prediction_failed", extra={"prediction_id": pid}) raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Prediction failed") from exc latency = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000 log_prediction(pid, req.model_dump(), category, confidence, latency) return TriageResponse( category=category, confidence=round(confidence, 4), needs_human=confidence < 0.75, # confidence gate model_version=artifacts["meta"]["version"], prediction_id=pid, latency_ms=round(latency, 2), ) @app.get("/health/ready") def readiness(): if "model" not in artifacts: raise HTTPException(503, "model not loaded") return {"status": "ready", "version": artifacts["meta"]["version"]} ``` Three elements make this production-shaped rather than a toy. The **confidence gate** routes uncertain cases to humans instead of guessing. The **`prediction_id`** returned to the caller is what enables outcome feedback later. And **separate health endpoints** let an orchestrator distinguish "starting" from "broken." ##### Phase 4: Containerize and deploy ```dockerfile FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN python -m venv /opt/venv && /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt FROM python:3.11-slim AS runtime ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH" RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* && useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv WORKDIR /app COPY --chown=appuser:appuser ./models ./models COPY --chown=appuser:appuser ./src ./src USER appuser EXPOSE 8000 HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --start-period=30s CMD curl -fsS localhost:8000/health/ready || exit 1 CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"] ``` ```bash gcloud run deploy ticket-triage \ --source . --region asia-south1 \ --memory 2Gi --min-instances 0 --max-instances 10 \ --allow-unauthenticated ``` `--min-instances 0` means the deployed service **costs nothing when idle** — which is what makes leaving a portfolio project running indefinitely practical. ##### Phase 5: Monitor ```python def log_prediction(pid: str, features: dict, category: str, confidence: float, latency_ms: float) -> None: db.execute( """INSERT INTO predictions (prediction_id, ts, model_version, features, category, confidence, latency_ms) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)""", (pid, datetime.now(timezone.utc), artifacts["meta"]["version"], json.dumps(features), category, confidence, latency_ms), ) @app.get("/v1/monitoring/summary") def monitoring_summary(hours: int = 24) -> dict: rows = db.query(""" SELECT category, COUNT(*) n, AVG(confidence) avg_conf, AVG(latency_ms) avg_latency FROM predictions WHERE ts > datetime('now', ?) GROUP BY category """, (f"-{hours} hours",)) current = [r["avg_conf"] for r in rows] return { "window_hours": hours, "total_predictions": sum(r["n"] for r in rows), "by_category": rows, "low_confidence_rate": db.scalar( "SELECT AVG(confidence < 0.75) FROM predictions WHERE ts > datetime('now', ?)", (f"-{hours} hours",)), "psi_vs_training": population_stability_index( TRAINING_CONFIDENCE_DIST, current), } ``` A simple monitoring endpoint plus a Streamlit page reading it is enough to demonstrate the capability. The **PSI against the training distribution** is the drift signal; the **low-confidence rate** tells you how much human review the system is generating. ##### Phase 6: CI/CD ```yaml name: CI/CD on: push: { branches: [main] } jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: { python-version: "3.11", cache: pip } - run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt - run: ruff check . && mypy src/ - run: pytest tests/ -q # unit + model contract + API tests deploy: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: production # approval gate steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2 with: workload_identity_provider: ${{ secrets.WIF_PROVIDER }} service_account: ${{ secrets.GCP_SA }} - run: gcloud run deploy ticket-triage --source . --region asia-south1 - name: Smoke test run: | curl -fsS --retry 8 --retry-delay 5 \ https://ticket-triage-xyz.run.app/health/ready ``` The essential tests, and they take an hour to write: ```python def test_model_beats_baseline(): assert model_f1 > baseline_f1 + 0.10 def test_feature_contract(): """Guards against training/serving column mismatch.""" assert set(build_features(SAMPLE).columns) == set(META["feature_columns"]) def test_api_rejects_invalid_input(): assert client.post("/v1/triage", json={**VALID, "prior_tickets": -5}).status_code == 422 def test_prediction_is_deterministic(): a = client.post("/v1/triage", json=VALID).json() b = client.post("/v1/triage", json=VALID).json() assert a["category"] == b["category"] ``` ##### The architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph DATA["Data"] A[(Source)] --> B[ETL + validation] B --> C[(Features
point-in-time)] end subgraph TRAIN["Training"] C --> D[Train pipeline] D --> E[Evaluate vs
baseline + champion] E --> F[(Model + metadata)] end subgraph SERVE["Serving"] F --> G[FastAPI + Docker] G --> H[Cloud Run
public HTTPS] H --> I[(Prediction log)] end subgraph OPS["Operations"] I --> J[Drift + confidence
monitoring] J -->|degradation| D K[GitHub Actions:
test → build → deploy] --> H end ``` Draw your own version of this. **A clear architecture diagram is the single most useful artefact in your README**, because it lets a reader understand the whole system in fifteen seconds. ##### Documentation The README is what a hiring manager reads. Structure it as problem, result, then detail: ```markdown # Support Ticket Triage Routes support tickets by category and urgency, escalating low-confidence cases to humans. **Macro-F1 0.87** (baseline 0.34), **p95 latency 84 ms**, ~₹340/month at 12k requests. 🔗 **Live demo:** https://ticket-triage-xyz.run.app/docs 🎥 **3-min walkthrough:** [link] ## Problem Agents spent ~3 minutes triaging each of ~400 daily tickets — roughly 20 hours a week of skilled time on routing rather than resolution. ## Results | Metric | Baseline | Model | |---|---|---| | Macro-F1 | 0.34 | **0.87** | | Triage time/ticket | 3 min | ~20 s (review only) | | Auto-routed (conf ≥ 0.75) | — | 71% | | p95 latency | — | 84 ms | ## Architecture [diagram] ## Key decisions - **XGBoost over a transformer**: 0.87 vs 0.89 F1, but 40× faster inference and no GPU needed. The two points did not justify the cost. - **Confidence gate at 0.75**: calibrated so escalated cases contain ~85% of the model's errors while sending only 29% of tickets to humans. - **Chronological split**: ticket categories shift seasonally; a random split overstated performance by 6 points. ## Limitations - Trained on English tickets only; Hindi and Hinglish are escalated by default. - Underperforms on the "billing" class (F1 0.71) — only 4% of training data. - No feedback loop yet: agent corrections are logged but not used for retraining. ## Run it locally \`\`\`bash git clone ... && cd ticket-triage cp .env.example .env # add your config docker compose up \`\`\` ``` The **limitations section** is counterintuitive and disproportionately effective. It signals that you evaluated your own work, and interviewers almost always ask about it — which means you control the hardest question. ##### Common mistakes - **Over-investing in modelling** and running out of time for deployment. - **No baseline**, so you cannot quantify the model's value. - **Random splits on temporal data**, overstating performance. - **A notebook as the deliverable** rather than a service. - **No public URL** — a link is worth more than a repository. - **Saving only the estimator** rather than the whole pipeline. - **No confidence gate**, so uncertain predictions are treated as certain. - **No prediction logging**, making monitoring impossible retrospectively. - **A README that leads with the tech stack** instead of the problem and result. - **Claiming no limitations**, which reads as not having looked. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **select a problem, build a working end-to-end solution from data to deployed model, and verify it runs in the cloud with a public endpoint.** Work the phases in order and time-box the modelling — set a deadline of one week and move on regardless of whether you have squeezed out the last point of accuracy. The mini project is the complete capstone: **deployed, accessible online, with monitoring.** The deployment is not the finishing touch; it is the deliverable. Everything before it is preparation. For the assignment, **write project documentation covering the problem, data, model choices, architecture, deployment and known limitations.** Include the architecture diagram, the before/after metrics table, and — most importantly — a section justifying two or three decisions with the alternatives you rejected. "XGBoost over a transformer: two points of F1 for 40× the inference cost" is engineering judgment on display, and it is what distinguishes a capstone from a tutorial follow-along. ##### Key takeaways - Deployment is the deliverable — a working URL with 87% accuracy demonstrates far more than a notebook with 96%. - Establish a baseline and choose your metric on day two; if the model cannot beat majority-class prediction, the problem is the data, not the algorithm. - Save the whole pipeline plus metadata, add a confidence gate for uncertain predictions, and return a prediction ID so outcomes can be linked later. - Ship the operational layer — logging, a drift check, health endpoints, CI with a smoke test — because that is what the course was actually teaching. - Lead the README with the problem and measured result, include an architecture diagram, justify your decisions with rejected alternatives, and document limitations honestly.
